claims.text: Adding small amounts of a secondary metal to a transition-metal catalyst can produce a moderate downshift of the active metal's d-band center.
The d-band-center shift can be varied while morphology, support, and particle size remain identical.
The d-band center is a governing descriptor of the adsorption strength of key reaction intermediates.
A more negative or downshifted d-band center weakens adsorbate binding.
Catalytic activity has a volcano-type dependence on d-band-center position, so an intermediate shift can optimize adsorption.
The electronic modification caused by alloying is a ligand effect.
Optimized intermediate binding promotes faster reaction turnover by balancing adsorption and desorption.
A moderate d-band-center downshift should improve catalytic activity relative to the pure-metal baseline.
A moderate d-band-center downshift should improve catalytic selectivity relative to the pure-metal baseline.
A moderate d-band-center downshift should improve catalyst durability relative to the pure-metal baseline.
Under moderate-temperature and moderate-pressure ORR or HER conditions, chemisorption and electronic effects dominate over mass transport and irreversible morphology changes.
Extreme alloying or conditions that cause substantial morphology changes may invalidate the predicted d-band trend.
Prior computational and spectroscopic evidence supports a correlation between d-band-center position and catalytic performance.
The optimal magnitude of the d-band-center shift and its performance effect vary with reaction and catalyst system.
XPS or operando XAS can quantitatively determine the d-band-center shift in the proposed catalyst series.
Failure of moderately downshifted catalysts to outperform the baseline would falsify the proposed governing role of the d-band-center shift.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis promises enhancement of activity, selectivity, and durability together, whereas the mechanism and predicted outcome weaken this to turnover, selectivity, or durability and to higher turnover frequency and/or lower overpotential.

The hypothesis and cited evidence invoke an optimum or volcano-type relationship, but the falsification rule asks for a direct correlation between the extent of the shift and performance. A volcano relationship need not be directly monotonic across the tested shift range.
